deletion_policy.description:
Whether Terraform will be prevented from destroying the instance. Defaults to "DELETE".
When a 'terraform destroy' or 'terraform apply' would delete the instance,
the command will fail if this field is set to "PREVENT" in Terraform state.
When set to "ABANDON", the command will remove the resource from Terraform
management without updating or deleting the resource in the API.
When set to "DELETE", deleting the resource is allowed.
deletion_policy.rationale: The destroy guard, and it defaults to DELETE. Destroying this resource does not break the load balancer; it quietly removes the extension from the request path, so traffic reverts to plain URL map routing and whatever the extension was doing stops happening, with no error anywhere to notice. ABANDON fails the other way, leaving the extension live in the data path but no longer tracked in code. Policy should pin this to the value that blocks destroys (PREVENT) so that pulling an extension out of a live load balancer is a deliberate, reviewed change rather than a side effect of a plan.

description.description: A human-readable description of the resource.
description.rationale: A human readable note. Nothing in the request path reads it, so constraining its wording would not change how the extension behaves.

forwarding_rules.description:
A list of references to the forwarding rules to which this service extension is attached to.
At least one forwarding rule is required. There can be only one LbRouteExtension resource per forwarding rule.
forwarding_rules.rationale: The load balancer forwarding rules this extension attaches to, and in effect which traffic it covers. Coverage gaps are a real risk, but any rule about them has to name a specific team's forwarding rules, which fails the generic test, and the one structural constraint that exists (a single route extension per forwarding rule) is already enforced by the API.

labels.description:
Set of labels associated with the LbRouteExtension resource.

**Note**: This field is non-authoritative, and will only manage the labels present in your configuration.
Please refer to the field 'effective_labels' for all of the labels present on the resource.
labels.rationale: Tags for grouping, filtering and cost attribution. Nothing in the data path consults them, and the field is not authoritative, since it manages only the labels listed in the configuration, so it could not serve as an enforcement point in any case.

load_balancing_scheme.description:
All backend services and forwarding rules referenced by this extension must share the same load balancing scheme.
For more information, refer to [Choosing a load balancer](https://cloud.google.com/load-balancing/docs/backend-service) and
[Supported application load balancers](https://cloud.google.com/service-extensions/docs/callouts-overview#supported-lbs). Possible values: ["INTERNAL_MANAGED", "EXTERNAL_MANAGED"]
load_balancing_scheme.rationale: Declares which scheme the referenced forwarding rules and backend services use, and they must all match or the API rejects the configuration. It does not decide whether the load balancer is exposed to the internet, since the forwarding rule does that, so pinning it cannot reduce exposure, and both accepted values are legitimate designs that a platform has no basis to choose between.

location.description: The location of the route extension
location.rationale: Determines the region/zone where the resource is created. Policy should restrict it to an approved-region whitelist for data residency; the allowed set is parameterised (a hardcoded example whitelist is acceptable).

name.description: Name of the LbRouteExtension resource in the following format: projects/{project}/locations/{location}/lbRouteExtensions/{lbRouteExtension}
name.rationale: The resource identifier, in a fixed projects/locations/lbRouteExtensions path format. It plays no part in matching, routing, or the call to the extension.

project.description: The ID of the project in which the resource belongs. If it is not provided, the provider project is used.
project.rationale: Which project owns the extension, defaulting to the provider project. Who may change it is enforced by that project's IAM and org policies rather than by this string, and no generic rule can name the correct project without being specific to one team.

extension_chains.description:
A set of ordered extension chains that contain the match conditions and extensions to execute.
Match conditions for each extension chain are evaluated in sequence for a given request.
The first extension chain that has a condition that matches the request is executed.
Any subsequent extension chains do not execute. Limited to 5 extension chains per resource.
Further information can be found at https://cloud.google.com/service-extensions/docs/reference/rest/v1/ExtensionChain

extension_chains.name.description:
The name for this extension chain. The name is logged as part of the HTTP request logs.
The name must conform with RFC-1034, is restricted to lower-cased letters, numbers and hyphens,
and can have a maximum length of 63 characters. Additionally, the first character must be a letter
and the last character must be a letter or a number.
extension_chains.name.rationale: An identifier for the chain, constrained in format by the API and written into the HTTP request logs. Useful for tracing which chain handled a request, but a naming rule is a convention rather than a security control.

extension_chains.extensions.description:
A set of extensions to execute for the matching request.
At least one extension is required. Up to 3 extensions can be defined for each extension chain for
LbTrafficExtension resource. LbRouteExtension chains are limited to 1 extension per extension chain.
Further documentation can be found at https://cloud.google.com/service-extensions/docs/reference/rest/v1/ExtensionChain#Extension

extension_chains.extensions.authority.description: The :authority header in the gRPC request sent from Envoy to the extension service.
extension_chains.extensions.authority.rationale: The :authority (host) header on the gRPC call the proxy makes to the callout service, required in practice for callout extensions, and effectively the hostname the extension backend sees. The correct value is whatever a team's own extension service expects, so no generic rule can supply it, and it grants nothing by itself: the trustworthiness of that hop comes from the callout backend service's own configuration.

extension_chains.extensions.fail_open.description:
Determines how the proxy behaves if the call to the extension fails or times out.
When set to TRUE, request or response processing continues without error.
Any subsequent extensions in the extension chain are also executed.
When set to FALSE: * If response headers have not been delivered to the downstream client,
a generic 500 error is returned to the client. The error response can be tailored by
configuring a custom error response in the load balancer.
extension_chains.extensions.fail_open.rationale: The switch between failing open and failing closed on the extension call, and it defaults to closed. Left false, an extension that fails or times out stops the request and the client gets a 500; set true, the request carries on as though the extension had never run and the rest of the chain executes anyway. Google's own guidance presents this as a trade off between security or integrity on one side and availability on the other, with closed as the preferred setting. Policy should require false, so an extension sitting in the request path cannot be bypassed simply by making it fail, and exceptions driven by availability should be documented exemptions.

extension_chains.extensions.forward_head.description:
List of the HTTP headers to forward to the extension (from the client or backend).
If omitted, all headers are sent. Each element is a string indicating the header name.
extension_chains.extensions.forward_head.rationale: Chooses which HTTP headers are handed to the extension service, and if it is left unset every header goes, including Authorization, Cookie and anything else the client sent. That is a decision about minimising the data given to a request path component that may be a callout backend, a Wasm plugin, or an endpoint managed by Google. Policy should require the list to be set explicitly rather than relying on the default that sends everything; which headers are needed stays a team decision.

extension_chains.extensions.metadata.description:
The metadata provided here is included as part of the 'metadata_context' (of type 'google.protobuf.Struct')
in the 'ProcessingRequest' message sent to the extension server.
The metadata is available under the namespace 'com.google.lb_route_extension.<resource_name>.<chain_name>.<extension_name>'.
The following variables are supported in the metadata: '{forwarding_rule_id}' - substituted with the forwarding rule's fully qualified resource name.
This field must not be set for plugin extensions. Setting it results in a validation error.
extension_chains.extensions.metadata.rationale: Operator defined configuration delivered to the team's own extension server inside the ProcessingRequest. Google's published example uses it to pass Model Armor template IDs. The contents are inherently specific to a workload, and it changes nothing about who can reach the load balancer or the extension. The one structural rule worth having, that it must not be set for plugin extensions, is already enforced by the API as a validation error.

extension_chains.extensions.name.description:
The name for this extension. The name is logged as part of the HTTP request logs.
The name must conform with RFC-1034, is restricted to lower-cased letters, numbers and hyphens,
and can have a maximum length of 63 characters. Additionally, the first character must be a letter
and the last a letter or a number.
extension_chains.extensions.name.rationale: An identifier for the extension, constrained in format by the API and logged with the HTTP request logs. It takes no part in matching, routing, or the extension call.

extension_chains.extensions.observabilit.description:
When set to 'TRUE', enables 'observability_mode' on the 'ext_proc' filter.
This makes 'ext_proc' calls asynchronous. Envoy doesn't check for the response from 'ext_proc' calls.
For more information about the filter, see: https://www.envoyproxy.io/docs/envoy/v1.32.3/api-v3/extensions/filters/http/ext_proc/v3/ext_proc.proto
This field is helpful when you want to try out the extension in async log-only mode.
Supported by regional 'LbTrafficExtension' and 'LbRouteExtension' resources.
Only 'STREAMED' (default) body processing mode is supported.
extension_chains.extensions.observabilit.rationale: Controls whether the extension runs in asynchronous observability mode, where Envoy sends ext_proc calls without waiting for or enforcing the extension response. This is an operational and architectural choice for passive or log-only integration rather than a security exposure or enforcement control. Platform policy should therefore not force observability mode on or off, leaving teams to choose the behaviour that fits their extension design.

extension_chains.extensions.service.description:
The reference to the service that runs the extension.

* To configure a callout extension, service must be a fully-qualified reference to a backend service.
* To configure a plugin extension, service must be a reference to a WasmPlugin resource.
extension_chains.extensions.service.rationale: Defines the backend service or WasmPlugin that executes the extension for matched traffic. Because this is the workload execution target for the extension, using an implicit, default, or inappropriate target can weaken least-privilege separation. Platform policy should require an explicit, non-default execution target without pinning a specific service or plugin name, so teams retain control over which approved workload performs the extension logic.

extension_chains.extensions.supported_ev.description:
A set of events during request or response processing for which this extension is called.
This field is optional for the LbRouteExtension resource. If unspecified, 'REQUEST_HEADERS' event is assumed as supported.
Possible values: 'REQUEST_HEADERS', 'REQUEST_BODY', 'REQUEST_TRAILERS'.
extension_chains.extensions.supported_ev.rationale: Defines which request lifecycle events, such as request headers, body, or trailers, cause the extension to run. Choosing these event hooks is a functional and architectural integration decision that depends on what each team's extension is designed to process. There is no universally secure event set for all workloads, so a platform policy that constrains these values would inappropriately dictate application design rather than enforce a generic security control.

extension_chains.extensions.timeout.description:
Specifies the timeout for each individual message on the stream. The timeout must be between 10-1000 milliseconds.
A duration in seconds with up to nine fractional digits, ending with 's'. Example: "3.5s".
extension_chains.extensions.timeout.rationale: Sets the per-message timeout for communication between the load balancer and the extension. The appropriate duration depends on workload latency, extension behaviour, performance requirements, and availability objectives. These are operational tuning choices rather than generic platform security controls, so teams should select the timeout that fits their service without a security policy imposing a universal threshold.

extension_chains.match_condition.description: Conditions under which this chain is invoked for a request.

extension_chains.match_condition.cel_exp.description: A Common Expression Language (CEL) expression that is used to match requests for which the extension chain is executed.
extension_chains.match_condition.cel_exp.rationale: Defines the free-form CEL expression used to decide which requests invoke the extension chain. The correct expression depends on team-specific routing, hosts, paths, headers, and application logic. A generic platform policy cannot meaningfully constrain arbitrary CEL logic without hardcoding or overreaching into workload-specific behaviour, so this free-form expression should remain a team-defined configuration rather than a platform security policy target.
